---
title: "Git: Save the History of Your Work"
description: "Create a local Git repository and practise a small, reviewable commit cycle."
categories: [Linux, Git, version control, command line]
---

## Learning goals

- I will be able to explain repository, working tree, stage, commit, and history.
- I will be able to create a repository and make small commits with useful messages.
- I will be able to inspect changes before saving or sharing them.

This is important because it enables me to experiment, explain what changed, and recover earlier work without creating files named `final-final-really-final`.

## Your first repository

Create a teacher-approved project folder inside your home directory. Configure Git with the classroom identity supplied by your teacher. Do not publish a personal email address.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/linux-labs/my-site
cd ~/linux-labs/my-site
git init
printf "# My Technology Site\n" > README.md
git status
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add project README"
git log --oneline
```

Repeat the cycle after making one small change: edit, `git status`, review, stage, review the staged change, commit, and inspect the history.

## Evidence

Submit the repository path, a screenshot of `git log --oneline`, and a six-step explanation of your commit cycle. Explain why a commit message should describe the change.

## Extend your learning

- Read [Getting started with Git](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/start-your-journey/hello-world).
- Use `git diff` to compare an uncommitted change with the last commit.

## Review and reflect

What is the difference between saving a file and committing it? At what point has Git recorded a recoverable checkpoint?
